title: Expected frequency
keyIdea: Expected frequency = probability × number of trials. A fair dice rolled 300 times should give about 1/6 × 300 = 50 sixes. It is a long-run average, not a promise: real results scatter round it, so 47 or 55 sixes are normal and exactly 50 is not even likely. With more trials the relative frequency (count ÷ trials) settles closer to the probability, even though the count can drift further from the expected number. A result far from expected, like 171 sixes in 600 rolls, is strong evidence that the dice is biased.
familyTip: Roll a real dice 60 times together and tally the sixes. Before you start, work out the expected number (10) and each write down a guess for what you will actually get. Then compare: being a few off is normal. Ask what you would think if you got 25.

visual.caption: Expected count for 120 rolls of a fair dice, or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: place expected sixes, work out P × trials, rerun 120 rolls, watch the proportion settle, and judge four dice.

kid: Expected frequency tells you how many times an outcome should happen, on average. Multiply its probability by the number of trials. A fair dice has P(six) = 1/6, so in 120 rolls you expect 1/6 × 120 = 20 sixes.
Expected does not mean exact. Roll 120 times and you might get 17 sixes, or 23. Do it again and you get a different number. Results scatter round the expected value. Hitting it exactly is quite rare.
More trials help. The fraction of sixes, count ÷ rolls, gets closer to 1/6 as the rolls go up. That fraction is the relative frequency. It is how we estimate a probability from an experiment.
You can use expected frequency to test a dice. In 600 rolls you expect 100 sixes. Getting 93 is normal. Getting 171 would be very unlikely with a fair dice, so the dice is probably biased.
adult: Ages 12 to 14. In England this is Key Stage 3 probability (relative frequency, and the expected results of experiments) and the GCSE content on expected outcomes. In the US it is Common Core 7.SP.C.6: approximate the probability of an event by collecting data and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability (for example, a number cube rolled 600 times gives about 200 rolls of 3 or 6).

The rule is E = p × n. It assumes independent trials with the same probability each time, which is why draws from a bag must be replaced. The probability comes first: for two coins, P(both heads) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, because HH, HT, TH and TT are equally likely; three outcomes (two heads, one of each, two tails) are not.

Observed counts vary. For 120 rolls the standard deviation of the number of sixes is about 4, so counts from roughly 12 to 28 are ordinary. As n grows the proportion settles (the law of large numbers), while the typical gap between the count and np grows like the square root of n. A gap of 71 in 600 rolls is nearly eight standard deviations, far beyond chance.

Common mistakes: expecting the exact value every time; using the number of faces or sections as the answer; using 1/2 for any two-way event; adding outcomes without checking they are equally likely; and calling a dice biased because one run was a few off. In the lab you place expected counts on a line, work out p × n in four contexts, repeat 120 rolls six times, compare 30, 300 and 3000 rolls, and judge four dice from 600 rolls each.

practice.prompt: A fair dice is rolled 300 times. How many sixes do you expect?
practice.hint: P(six) = 1/6. Multiply by the number of rolls.
practice.explain: Expected = 1/6 × 300 = 50. 6 is the number of faces, and 150 would be P = 1/2.

practice.prompt: A fair dice is rolled {=6*n} times. How many 4s do you expect?
You expect 20 sixes in 120 rolls but get 17. What does this show?
choices: Normal variation: real results scatter round expected
The expected value was worked out wrong
practice.hint: Do results have to equal the expected value?
practice.explain: 1/6 × 120 = 20 is right, and a gap of 3 is very common with a fair dice. It is not evidence of bias.

practice.prompt: A spinner has {k} equal parts, and 1 of them is blue. It is spun {=k*n} times. How many blues do you expect?
practice.hint: P(blue) = 1/{k}. Multiply by the number of spins.

practice.prompt: Two coins are tossed 80 times. How often do you expect both to land heads?
practice.hint: List the outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT.
practice.explain: P(both heads) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, so expect 1/4 × 80 = 20. 40 uses P = 1/2, and 27 wrongly treats three outcomes as equally likely.

pool.prompt: P(rain) = 0.3 on any day. How many rainy days do you expect in 30 days?
pool.hint: Multiply the probability by the number of days.
pool.explain: 0.3 × 30 = 9. 3 confuses the probability with a count, and 10 would be P = 1/3.

pool.prompt: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue counters. You take one and put it back, 50 times. Expected reds?
pool.hint: P(red) = 3 out of how many counters?
pool.explain: P(red) = 3/10, so expect 3/10 × 50 = 15. 21 uses 3/7, but there are 10 counters.

pool.prompt: Which gives the most reliable estimate of P(six) for a dice?
choices: The proportion of sixes in 3000 rolls
pool.hint: Which sample has the most trials? Bigger samples are steadier.
pool.explain: More trials make the relative frequency settle closer to the true probability, so 3000 rolls is most reliable.

pool.prompt: A dice gives 171 sixes in 600 rolls. What is the best conclusion?
choices: It is probably biased towards six
It is fair: results always vary
pool.hint: Expected is 100. How far off is 171?
pool.explain: 171 is 71 above the expected 100, far more than chance usually allows, so the dice is probably biased. Probability evidence never makes it certain.

pool.prompt: Is it surprising to get exactly 50 heads in 100 fair tosses?
choices: No, but it happens less than 1 time in 10
No, it happens almost every time
pool.hint: Exactly 50 is the single most likely count, but there are many other counts.
pool.explain: Exactly 50 heads has probability about 0.08. It is the most likely single count, yet most runs land a little above or below.

pool.prompt: P(late) = 0.{d} on any school day. How many late days do you expect in 100 days?
pool.hint: Multiply the probability 0.{d} by the 100 days.

pool.prompt: A fair coin is tossed {=2*n} times. You get {=n+h} heads. How many more than expected is that?
pool.explain: Expected = 1/2 × {=2*n} = {n}, so {=n+h} heads is {h} more than expected.

pool.prompt: Expected frequency for rolling an even number in 90 fair dice rolls?
pool.hint: How many even faces are there on a dice?
pool.explain: Even faces are 2, 4 and 6, so P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2 and expect 1/2 × 90 = 45.

pool.prompt: Why must counters be put back before the next draw when finding an expected frequency?
choices: So the probability stays the same each time
pool.hint: E = p × n needs the same p for every trial.
pool.explain: Replacing the counter keeps P(red) the same on every draw, which is what the rule p × n assumes.
